docs.title: SupplyNetBench
docs.text:
A large collection of simulated supply chains. Each one is a small world of suppliers, factories, warehouses, shops and customers, run day by day for five years on a computer. For every supply chain the dataset stores its full description (who supplies whom, and every number that controls it) together with what happened in the simulation (how much was sold, how much stock was held, how much money was made or lost).

The dataset is made with SupplyNetPy, an open-source supply-chain simulator from IIT Goa 1.

Numbers on this page come from the build demo_v2 (generator 0.7.0, created 2026-10-17 04:26:56).

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
• Many different supply chains. Thousands of network shapes, from 10 to about 300 nodes. Most are layered like real chains (suppliers → factories → warehouses → shops → customers); some are random trees that test unusual shapes. See How a network is built.
  • Four industries. Groceries, electronics, medicines and industrial spare parts. Every network is run once for each industry, with numbers typical of that industry (delivery times, prices, order sizes). See How the numbers are chosen.
  • Good times and bad times. Some setups are run well, others badly on purpose (wrong forecasts, price wars, broken factories). This makes sure the data contains failures, not only success.
  • Matched "what-if" pairs. Some setups have copies that differ in exactly one thing (a breakdown, a smaller factory, a different safety stock). The customers are the same, so any difference is caused by that one change. See How a simulation runs.
  • Ready for machine learning. Every network is already put into a training, validation or test group, and a loader turns each setup into graph arrays. See Finding your way around.

docs.title: Why it is needed
docs.text:
Running a detailed supply-chain simulation takes seconds to minutes. A planner who wants to compare thousands of designs ("Should we add a warehouse? Which supplier should we drop?") cannot wait that long for each one. A machine-learning model trained on many simulated chains could give an answer in milliseconds. Graph neural networks are a natural fit, because a supply chain is a graph 2.

Such a model needs a large, varied and honest training set:

  • Large, so it sees enough examples.
  • Varied, so it learns about shape, industry and policy, not one fixed case.
  • Honest, so every number is internally consistent and every assumption is written down.

Real company data is private, small and never covers "what if". Simulation fills that gap.

This dataset builds on the GNN supply-chain dataset of Lone and Karanjkar 2. It adds larger and deeper networks, four industries, disruptions, seasonal demand, deliberately badly run setups, what-if pairs and the day-by-day history of every run.

docs.title: How it is made
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["1. Pick a size<br/>(number of nodes)"] --> B["2. Build a network<br/>(who supplies whom)"]
    B --> C["3. Fill in the numbers<br/>(demand, stock rules,<br/>prices, delays)"]
    C --> D["4. Simulate 5 years<br/>with SupplyNetPy"]
    D --> E["5. Measure results<br/>(sales, stock, profit)"]
    E --> F["6. Save as tables<br/>(Parquet files)"]
  1. Pick a size. A number of nodes between 10 and 150 (a few up to 300).
  2. Build the network. Place suppliers, factories, warehouses and shops, then connect them.
  3. Fill in every number. Customer demand comes first. Every other number (stock levels, factory size, prices) is worked out from the flow of goods that site must carry, so nothing is random on its own.
  4. Simulate. SupplyNetPy plays out 1,825 days, order by order and delivery by delivery.
  5. Measure. The first year is thrown away (warm-up). The next four years give the results.
  6. Save. Inputs and results are written as typed tables that can be filtered without loading everything.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
A scenario generator, not a copy of real companies

The numbers are chosen to be plausible and varied, not fitted to any real company. A few of them are checked against public figures (for example, the median inventory carrying cost of 10% a year reported by APQC 3). The rest are reasoned design choices. Every one of them is listed in Assumptions and limits. Do not read the results as forecasts for a real business.

docs.text: What Value Networks (distinct shapes) 6,170 (5,709) Setups (configs) 20,619, of which 13,721 base and 6,898 what-if copies Simulations (runs) 29,175 (0 failed) Network size 10–265 nodes, middle (median) 37 Industries Groceries (FMCG), Electronics, Medicines (pharma), Industrial spare parts Simulated time per run 1,825 days (5 years), first 365 days are warm-up Train / validation / test 69% / 16% / 15% of networks Size on disk 1.01 GB (0.89 GB of it is the day-by-day history) Generator version 0.7.0 (SupplyNetPy 0.2.2)

docs.title: Who made it
docs.text:
B.Tech project at IIT Goa by Ashwin Gaikwad, guided by Tushar Lone and Prof. Neha Karanjkar.

  1. T. Lone and N. Karanjkar, "SupplyNetPy: An Open-Source Python Library for High-Fidelity Modeling and Simulation of Arbitrary Supply Chain and Inventory Networks", arXiv:2607.09745, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09745 ↩

  2. T. Lone and N. Karanjkar, "On the Potential of Graph Neural Networks as Metamodels for Supply Chain Optimization: Dataset, Architectures, and Directions", arXiv:2607.16769, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16769 ↩↩

  3. APQC, "Inventory carrying cost as a percentage of inventory value" (measure 100784, 6,468 organisations). https://www.apqc.org/what-we-do/benchmarking/open-standards-benchmarking/measures/inventory-carrying-cost-percentage ↩

docs.title: Assumptions and limits
docs.text: Every simulation simplifies the real world. This page lists what is simplified, why, and what it means for anyone using the data. A longer list, with every number and its status, is kept in check.md in the repository.

docs.title: What kind of data this is
docs.text:
The dataset is a scenario generator, partly anchored to public evidence. It is not fitted to any real company or industry:

  • A handful of numbers are compared with dated public figures (table below).
  • Every other number is a reasoned design choice: a range we judge plausible, kept wide on purpose for variety, and open to change when better evidence arrives.

The results should be read as "what this kind of network tends to do under these rules", not as a forecast for a real business.

docs.title: Main assumptions
docs.text: # Assumption Why What it means for users 1 One product. Every factory makes the same product Keeps each network readable and matches SupplyNetPy's one-product-per-site model Results say nothing about product mixes or shared capacity between products 2 Lost sales. Customers take what is on the shelf; the rest is lost Common in retail; avoids an edge case in customer waiting Fill rate is "served at once"; there are no customer backorders 3 Sites wait for supplies. Orders between sites wait until they can be shipped in full SupplyNetPy behaviour A short supplier delays its children instead of cancelling their orders 4 Planners plan for normal days. Stock rules ignore season, growth and breakdowns Many real plans do the same; it creates realistic stress Seasonal peaks and long breakdowns cause shortages by design 5 Factories are sized for normal demand (60%–97% busy) Deliberate stress 61% of factories cannot keep up at their seasonal peak (peak_load > 1) 6 Unlimited storage space at factories, warehouses and shops Keeps the focus on flow, not floor space Stock is limited only by the stock rule 7 Breakdowns stop new orders, but goods already on the road still arrive SupplyNetPy behaviour A breakdown hurts after a delay, as stock runs down 8 Whole-number recipes (1–3 units of each raw material) Avoids a rounding edge case in the library — 9 Fixed supplier weights for sites with two suppliers Simple, common practice No smart switching between suppliers, except skipping one that is broken down 10 Money without currency. Each setup has its own price units Industries differ by orders of magnitude Compare ratios (margin, cost shares), not absolute money across setups 11 Stress setups are badly run on purpose (80%) So the data contains failures Use the regime column to separate them from the well-run 20%

docs.title: Checked against public figures
docs.text:
Each of these is a comparison, not a fit: the public figure and our number do not always measure exactly the same thing.

Topic Public figure Our number Holding cost APQC median: 10% of inventory value per year, 6,468 organisations 1 10%–40% a year (lower end matches the median) Fill rate APQC median order fill rate: 94% 2 Control setups: median fill 0.94–0.98. APQC counts whole orders, we count units, so this is only a rough comparison Factory use RBI: Indian manufacturing ran at 74.6% of capacity, Q1 2026-27 3 Factories busy 60%–97% on a normal day Medicine margins NPPA ceiling price = price to retailer × 1.16, i.e. a 13.8% margin 4 Used to sense-check pharma shop margins Stores per warehouse DMart: 415 stores, 75 DCs, about 5.5 stores per DC 5 About 6 shops per warehouse in layered networks Long breakdowns Renesas Naka fire: about 97 days to full production 6 Breakdowns last days to weeks on average, with a rare long tail Logistics cost India: 7.97% of GDP, 2023-24 7 Freight 0.3%–3% of goods value per leg (different measure; comparison only)

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Three warehouse layers are rare (about 1% of layered networks), below the 10% target.
  • Large networks are few: about 5% of sizes are above 150 nodes.
  • Rare long zero-sales spells. A small number of runs sell nothing for several months, after a very long breakdown of a factory's only supplier. This is allowed by the breakdown model, not a fault, but users who want "normal" runs may filter on main_outage_days.
  • Not modelled: several products, customer waiting, transport capacity, partial breakdowns (a site working at half speed), long electronics purchasing times, and quality-control delays in medicines. These are candidates for later versions.

docs.title: Fixed in this version
docs.text:
Version 0.7.1 fixes a stall found in the demo build: after a breakdown, a factory could place one raw-material order larger than its limited supplier's whole store. SupplyNetPy ships orders whole, so that order could never be filled and the network stopped selling. Limited suppliers' stores are now always at least as large as the largest order a factory can place (How the numbers are chosen).

  1. APQC, measure 100784. https://www.apqc.org/what-we-do/benchmarking/open-standards-benchmarking/measures/inventory-carrying-cost-percentage ↩

  2. APQC, "Order fill rate", measure 101445. https://www.apqc.org/what-we-do/benchmarking/open-standards-benchmarking/measures/order-fill-rate ↩

  3. Reserve Bank of India, OBICUS. https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/PublicationsView.aspx?id=24087 ↩

  4. National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority, proactive disclosure on ceiling-price method. https://www.nppa.gov.in/en/proactivedisclosure ↩

  5. Avenue Supermarts (DMart), Annual Report FY2024-25. https://www.msei.in/SX-Content/Listing/Annual-Reports/2025/DMART-2025.pdf ↩

  6. Renesas Electronics, Naka Factory fire update, 2021. https://www.renesas.com/en/about/press-room/update-10-notice-regarding-semiconductor-manufacturing-factory-naka-factory-fire-production-capacity ↩

  7. DPIIT and NCAER, Assessment of Logistics Cost in India, 2025. https://www.dpiit.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/09/c0d7c33f0b737ed71728ff6c2a35f1e7.pdf ↩

docs.title: Three words to know
docs.text:
Word In the code Meaning How many Network graph The map of who supplies whom Up to 50 per size Setup config One network with all its numbers, for one industry 4 per network, plus what-if copies Run run One 5-year simulation of a setup 1 per setup (5 for 10% of them)

On average, one network gives 4 base setups and about 8 runs.

docs.title: How the files are organised
docs.text:
Everything is stored as Parquet tables 1. Parquet is a compressed, column-based format that Python (pyarrow, pandas, polars), R and Spark can all read. A reader can load only the columns and rows it needs. Each table is a folder of files:

dataset/
├── meta.json          all build settings, versions and counts
├── graphs/            one row per network
├── configs/           one row per setup
├── nodes/             one row per node of each setup (its numbers)
├── edges/             one row per link of each setup
├── demands/           one row per customer stream of each setup
├── runs/              one row per run: the main catalogue and network results
├── node_results/      one row per run × node: node results
├── series/            one row per run: the day-by-day history (large; optional)
└── SHA256SUMS         checksums, to check that a download is complete

erDiagram
    graphs ||--o{ configs : "graph_id"
    configs ||--o{ nodes : "config_id"
    configs ||--o{ edges : "config_id"
    configs ||--o{ demands : "config_id"
    configs ||--o{ runs : "config_id"
    runs ||--o{ node_results : "run_id"
    runs ||--o| series : "run_id"

Every id is a whole number. A node's id is its position in the network (0 … n−1) and is the same in every table. The files are sorted by split and industry, so reading only "test, pharma" skips everything else.

The day-by-day history is optional

The series/ folder holds most of the bytes. If you only need the summary results, skip it when downloading. The loader never reads it unless asked.

docs.title: graphs: one row per network
docs.text: Column Meaning graph_id Network id topology echelon (layered) or random_tree roles One letter per node: S supplier, M factory, I warehouse or shop, D customers src, dst All links, as two lists (link k goes from src[k] to dst[k]) n, s, m, i, d Number of nodes, and of each kind depth Longest path from a supplier to a customer dc_tiers Number of warehouse layers (layered networks) multi_parent Number of nodes with more than one supplier size_band base (up to 150 nodes) or large split train, val or test graph_hash, dup_of Fingerprint; id of the first network with the same fingerprint

docs.title: configs: one row per setup
docs.text: Column Meaning config_id, graph_id Setup id, its network scenario Industry: fmcg, electronics, pharma, industrial regime stress (badly run on purpose) or control (well run) base_config_id Equal to config_id for a base setup; for a what-if copy, the id of its base variant, variant_node, variant_start, variant_value The what-if change: kind (outage, capacity, service), where, when, how much setup-wide settings margin_factor, service_mean, bias_mean, season_amp, trend, outage_p, finite_supply, holding_rate_year, …

docs.title: nodes, edges, demands: the numbers of each setup
docs.text:
• nodes: one row per node. Its flow per day, forecast, delivery time, stock rule (s, S, Q, review), safety factor, factory batch size, supplier rate and store, breakdown rates, prices and costs.
  • edges: one row per link: average delivery time and its spread, order share, cost per order.
  • demands: one row per customer stream: units per day, orders per day, order size, season, growth.

docs.title: runs: one row per run
docs.text: The catalogue. Each row repeats the most useful setup columns (industry, size, regime, split, what-if kind), so most filtering needs this table only. It also holds the network results listed in How a simulation runs, the warm-up check, run time and status (ok or error).

docs.title: node_results: one row per run × node
docs.text: Each node's own results over the measured years: fill rate, demand, shortage, shipped, average stock, money in and out, breakdown days, observed delivery time.

docs.title: series: one row per run
docs.text:
Eight lists of 1,825 daily values: cust_demand, cust_served, ext_revenue, net_cost, profit, book_profit (amounts for that day), and inventory, site_backorder (levels at the end of the day). Day 1 is the first element; the first 365 days are the warm-up.

Units of every column are stored inside the files (Parquet metadata key units).

docs.title: Where to get it
docs.text:
The dataset will be published on Hugging Face (link to be added). The code that builds it is in this repository, so the dataset can be rebuilt exactly from the same seed.

  1. Apache Parquet. https://parquet.apache.org/ ↩

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms used in these pages and in the column names, in alphabetical order.

Term Meaning Base setup A setup without a what-if change. Its base_config_id equals its config_id. Batch The amount a factory makes in one go. One batch at a time, so the batch size sets the factory's capacity. Breakdown (outage) A period when a supplier, factory or warehouse takes no new orders. Config The code's word for a setup. Control setup A well-run setup: honest forecasts, normal prices, a 90%–98% service target. 20% of setups. Customer stream (D) The flow of customer orders at one shop. DC (distribution centre) A warehouse between factories and shops. Delivery time (lead time) Days from placing an order to receiving it. Echelon / layer One level of the chain: suppliers, factories, a warehouse layer, shops. A layered (echelon) network has goods flowing level by level. EOQ Economic order quantity: the order size that balances the cost of ordering against the cost of holding stock. Fill rate The share of demand served at once from the shelf. 1.0 means every unit was served. Flow The average number of units a site passes on per day. FMCG Fast-moving consumer goods, such as groceries and toiletries. Forecast bias How far the planner's demand estimate is from the truth. Negative means too low. Graph The code's word for a network. Holding cost The cost of keeping stock: money tied up, storage, insurance, spoilage. Given as a share of the stock's value per year. Lost sale Demand that could not be served from the shelf and is gone. Customers here never wait. Margin Profit divided by sales. MSER-5 An automatic test for the length of the warm-up period of a simulation. Network The map of who supplies whom. Node One point in the network: a supplier, factory, warehouse, shop or customer stream. Parquet The file format of the tables: compressed, by column, readable from most data tools. Peak load How busy a factory is at the seasonal peak, compared with its capacity. Above 1 means it cannot keep up. Recipe Units of each raw material needed for one unit of product (1–3). Regime stress or control. Replication (repeat) Another run of the same setup with different random luck. Review period (r) How often a site checks its stock: every day or every week. Run One 5-year simulation of a setup. (s, S) rule The stock rule: when the stock position falls to s or below, order up to S. Safety factor (z) How much extra stock is kept for surprises, in units of demand uncertainty. Higher z, fewer shortages. Scenario The code's word for industry: fmcg, electronics, pharma, industrial. Seed The starting number for all randomness. Same seed, same dataset. Series The day-by-day history of a run. Service target The chance of not running out during one reorder cycle that a site aims for. It sets z. Setup One network with all its numbers filled in, for one industry. Shop (retailer) A site that sells to customers. Skip link A link that jumps over a layer, for example factory straight to shop. Split The machine-learning group of a network: train, val or test. Stock position Stock on the shelf + stock on its way − stock still owed to others. Stress setup A setup that may be badly run on purpose (wrong forecasts, price wars, low stock). 80% of setups. Supplier, finite / infinite A finite supplier produces at a fixed rate into a limited store and can run out. An infinite one never runs out. Warm-up The first simulated year. It is left out of the results because the full starting shelves make it unrealistic. What-if copy (variant) A copy of a base setup with one change (breakdown, smaller factory, different safety stock) and the same random luck.

docs.title: Finding your way around
docs.text: This page shows how to open the dataset, pick the part you need, and turn it into arrays for a model. All examples are in Python.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/AshwinG-23/supplynetbench.git
cd supplynetbench
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r generator/requirements.txt pandas

Download the dataset into, say, data/v2. Skip the series/ folder if you do not need the day-by-day history. After downloading, check that nothing is missing:

cd data/v2 && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS

In Python, make the helper code importable:

import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "generator")
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from dataset import query
from loader import load_graphs, to_pyg, load_series, aggregate

docs.title: Filter and sort the catalogue
docs.text:
query(root, filter, table, columns) reads one table and keeps only matching rows. The filter is applied while reading, so the rest of the file is never loaded.

# All finished medicine runs, as a pandas table
runs = query("data/v2", (pc.field("scenario") == "pharma") & (pc.field("status") == "ok")).to_pandas()

# Badly served networks: fill rate below 0.7
bad = runs[runs.main_fill < 0.7]

# Sort by profit per day, best first
runs.sort_values("main_profit_day", ascending=False).head()

Useful columns to filter on (all in the runs table):

Filter by Column Values Industry scenario fmcg, electronics, pharma, industrial Machine-learning group split train, val, test Well or badly run regime control, stress Network size n 10 … ~300 Network shape topology, depth, multi_parent echelon / random_tree, numbers Big networks only size_band base, large Base setups only variant null for base setups What-if copies variant, base_config_id outage, capacity, service Runs that passed the warm-up check warmup_ok True / False Breakdowns main_outage_days 0 = no breakdown

More examples:

# Large layered networks in the test group
big = query("data/v2", (pc.field("size_band") == "large") & (pc.field("split") == "test"))

# Every what-if pair: join each copy to its base
r = query("data/v2", columns=["run_id", "config_id", "base_config_id", "replication", "variant", "main_fill"]).to_pandas()
base = r[r.variant.isna()]
pairs = r[r.variant.notna()].merge(base, left_on=["base_config_id", "replication"],
                                   right_on=["config_id", "replication"], suffixes=("", "_base"))
pairs["fill_change"] = pairs.main_fill - pairs.main_fill_base

# The numbers of one setup's nodes
nodes = query("data/v2", pc.field("config_id") == 42, table="nodes").to_pandas()

docs.title: Graph arrays for machine learning
docs.text:
load_graphs gives one Python dict per setup, with NumPy arrays ready for a graph neural network:

for g in load_graphs("data/v2", split="train", scenario="pharma"):
    g["x"]            # [nodes, features]  node inputs (stock rule, prices, delivery times, node kind, ...)
    g["edge_index"]   # [2, links]         who supplies whom
    g["edge_attr"]    # [links, features]  delivery time, its spread, order share, cost
    g["y_node"]       # [runs, nodes, 5]   node results: fill, avg_inventory, shortage, revenue, cost
    g["y_graph"]      # [runs, 5]          network results: fill, profit_day, margin, ext_revenue_day, avg_inventory
    g["meta"]         # ids, industry, regime, what-if change

With PyTorch Geometric 1 installed, to_pyg(g) turns it into a Data object.

docs.title: The day-by-day history
docs.text:
s = load_series("data/v2", split="test", scenario="pharma",
                columns=["cust_demand", "cust_served", "profit"], days="main")   # warm-up dropped
s["run_id"]        # [runs]
s["profit"]        # [runs, days]  float32
w = aggregate(s, 7)   # weekly totals (use 30 for roughly monthly)

Only the asked-for columns, runs and days are read from disk.

docs.title: Check the files yourself
docs.text:
generator/.venv/bin/python generator/loader.py data/v2

This checks that the tables join correctly and that the daily history adds up to the summary results.

  1. M. Fey and J. E. Lenssen, "Fast Graph Representation Learning with PyTorch Geometric", ICLR Workshop, 2019. https://pyg.org/ ↩

docs.title: How a network is built
docs.text:
A network is the map of who supplies whom. It has five kinds of node:

Letter Node What it does S Supplier Provides one raw material M Factory (manufacturer) Turns raw materials into the product I Warehouse (DC) or shop Holds stock and sells it on D Customers A stream of customer orders at one shop

There is a single product. Every factory makes the same product, and every warehouse and shop stocks it. Goods flow from suppliers down to customers; orders flow the other way.

The code for this page is in generator/topology.py and generator/dataset.py.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Pick a size n<br/>(10–150 nodes, a few up to 300)"] --> B{"Pick a shape family"}
    B -- "75%" --> C["Layered network"]
    B -- "25%" --> D["Random tree"]
    C --> E["Up to 50 different networks of size n"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Remove repeats"]
    F --> G["Put each network in<br/>train, validation or test"]

docs.title: 1. Pick the size
docs.text:
The size n (number of nodes) is a whole number from 10 to 150. It is drawn on a log scale, so small and large sizes are equally common in ratio terms: 10–20 nodes is as likely as 75–150 nodes. This gives many small, cheap networks and still a good number of big ones.

About 5% of sizes are drawn again between 150 and 300 nodes and marked size_band = large. They test whether a model trained on smaller networks still works on bigger ones.

docs.title: 2. Pick the shape family
docs.text:
• Layered network (75%). Suppliers → factories → 0 to 3 layers of warehouses → shops → customers. This is how most real supply chains are organised 1.
  • Random tree (25%). A tree (each node has one supplier) of any shape, drawn so that every possible tree with that mix of node types is equally likely. These are often deep and thin, and serve as an "unusual shape" test.

docs.title: 3. Build a layered network
docs.text:
1. How many warehouse layers. 0, 1, 2 or 3 layers, with chances 20%, 40%, 30% and 10%.
  2. How wide each layer is. Each layer is 2 to 20 times wider than the layer above it. Then all layers are shrunk by the same factor until the total equals n exactly. A warehouse layer that becomes too thin is dropped. There are 0.7 to 2.5 suppliers per factory.
  3. One supplier for every site. Every node gets one supplier in the layer above. Some suppliers get many children and some only a few, as in real life ("rich get richer" choice).

  4. Extra links. The chance of each kind of extra link is drawn separately for each network:

    Extra link What it means Chance per site Second supplier A warehouse or shop buys from two places in the layer above 10%–30% Skip link A site buys from two or more layers up, for example factory → shop 0%–8% Shared supplier A factory also uses a supplier that already serves another factory 5%–30% Warehouse with own customers A warehouse also sells straight to customers 0%–15%

  5. Customers. Every shop gets one customer stream.

![A small layered network](img/example_small.png) A small layered network: two suppliers, one factory, one warehouse layer and seven shops. Several shops buy from both warehouses. ![A medium layered network](img/example_medium.png) A medium layered network. Note the skip links (factory straight to a shop). ![A random tree](img/example_tree.png) A random tree: every node has exactly one supplier.

docs.title: 4. Remove repeats
docs.text: For each size, up to 50 different networks are made. Two networks count as the same if they have the same shape and the same node types in the same places. This is checked with a graph fingerprint, the Weisfeiler–Lehman hash 2. Within one draw, repeats are thrown away. The same size can be drawn more than once, so a network can still match one from another draw. Such a network is kept, but marked in the dup_of column with the id of the first copy, so it is easy to skip.

docs.title: 5. Split for machine learning
docs.text: Each network goes to training (70%), validation (15%) or testing (15%). The choice comes from the network's fingerprint, so identical networks always land in the same group. A model is therefore never tested on a network shape it was trained on.

docs.title: How often each feature appears
docs.text:
Feature Share Layered network / random tree 77% / 23% of networks Warehouse layers 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 (layered networks) 24% / 57% / 17% / 1% At least one node with two or more suppliers 96.4% of layered networks Large networks (over 150 nodes) 7.3% of networks Suppliers that can run out 50.6% of setups Sites that can break down 60.3% of setups Seasonal demand 69.4% of setups Stress / control setups 80.0% / 20.0% Base setups with what-if copies 25.1%

Known gap

Three warehouse layers are rarer than planned, because the shrinking step in 3.2 often drops the thinnest layer. A fix is planned for a later version.

  1. S. Chopra and P. Meindl, Supply Chain Management: Strategy, Planning, and Operation, Pearson (any recent edition), chapter on designing distribution networks. ↩

  2. N. Shervashidze, P. Schweitzer, E. J. van Leeuwen, K. Mehlhorn and K. M. Borgwardt, "Weisfeiler-Lehman Graph Kernels", Journal of Machine Learning Research 12, 2011. As implemented in NetworkX: https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/generated/networkx.algorithms.graph_hashing.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash.html ↩

docs.title: How the numbers are chosen
docs.text:
Once the network is fixed, every node and link needs numbers: how much customers buy, how long deliveries take, when to reorder, how big the factory is, what things cost. This page explains where each number comes from. The code is configure() in generator/chain.py.

The main idea: customers first, everything else follows

Customer demand is drawn first. It is then pushed up the network, so each site knows how much it must carry on a normal day. Stock levels, factory size, prices and freight are all worked out from that flow. A big shop therefore gets a big stock and a busy factory gets a big machine. Nothing is random on its own, so the numbers always fit together.

docs.title: The order of filling
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    K["0. Setup-wide settings<br/>(industry, good or bad management,<br/>season, growth, breakdown risk)"] --> D
    D["1. Customer demand<br/>at every shop"] --> F["2. Flow pushed upstream<br/>(each site's normal daily load)"]
    F --> L["3. Delivery times<br/>on every link"]
    L --> P["4. Prices<br/>(factory → shop)"]
    P --> S["5. Stock rule at every site<br/>(reorder level, order size)"]
    S --> C["6. Factory capacity"]
    C --> U["7. Limited suppliers"]
    U --> O["8. Breakdowns"]

docs.title: 0. Setup-wide settings
docs.text:
Before any node is filled, a few settings are drawn once for the whole setup. They are stored in the configs table.

  • Industry: groceries (FMCG), electronics, medicines (pharma) or industrial spare parts. Each industry has its own number ranges (table below).
  • Stress or control. 80% of setups are stress setups: they may forecast badly, run price wars or aim for low stock levels, so failures happen. 20% are control setups: honest forecasts, normal prices and a 90%, 95% or 98% service target, the usual range in practice 3. The regime column tells them apart.
  • Season (70% of setups): demand goes up and down once a year, usually by up to ±50% (a few streams up to ±75%).
  • Growth: demand grows or shrinks by −10% to +20% a year.
  • Breakdown risk (60% of setups): some sites break down now and then.
  • Limited suppliers (50% of setups): some suppliers can run out.

docs.title: 1. Customer demand
docs.text:
Each customer stream gets:

Number How it is chosen Average units per day Drawn around the industry's typical value (a log-normal spread) Orders per day Drawn from the industry's range. Average order size = units ÷ orders Order size Varies around its average. How much it varies depends on the industry (industrial orders are the lumpiest) Season and growth The setup's season and growth, with a small change per stream

Customers arrive at random times (a Poisson process 1), faster in the busy season. A customer takes what is on the shelf. If the shelf is short, the rest of the order is lost. Customers never wait.

docs.title: 2. Flow pushed upstream
docs.text:
Each site's flow is the average number of units it must pass on per day:

  • A shop's flow = its customers' demand.
  • A warehouse's flow = the share of its children's flow that it supplies.
  • A factory's flow = what its warehouses take from it.
  • A supplier's flow = the factory's flow × units of raw material per product (the recipe, 1 to 3).

A site with two suppliers splits its orders at random with fixed weights. The main supplier gets 50% to 90% of orders.

docs.title: 3. Delivery times
docs.text: Every link gets a delivery time drawn from its industry's range (table below). Each shipment's actual time varies around that average (a gamma distribution), by an amount that is also drawn per setup. A factory needs all its raw materials, so its planning time is the longest of its inbound deliveries, plus the time to make a batch.

docs.title: 4. Prices
docs.text:
• Suppliers sell raw material at a price from the industry range.
  • A factory's cost per unit = raw materials + making cost.
  • The shop price is the factory cost × a markup. The markup is drawn per setup and split along the chain between the factory, the warehouses and the shop.
  • Stress setups may squeeze the markup almost to zero (a price war), so some of them lose money.
  • Holding cost: keeping one unit in stock for a year costs 10% to 40% of its value. The lower end matches the median measured by APQC across 6,468 organisations 5.
  • Freight: each delivery costs a fixed amount plus a small share (0.3% to 3%) of the value of the goods.

docs.title: 5. Stock rule at every site
docs.text:
Every factory, warehouse and shop follows the (s, S) rule, the standard textbook stock rule 2:

Check stock every r days. If the stock position has fallen to the reorder level s or below, order enough to bring it back up to the order-up-to level S.

The stock position is the stock on the shelf, plus what is already on its way, minus what is still owed to others.

How s and S are worked out:

  1. Forecast. The planner's estimate of daily demand. In stress setups it is often too low (by up to about 50%). In control setups it is right on average.

  2. Cover for the delivery time. s must cover the forecast demand during the delivery time plus the review period, plus a safety margin for surprises:

    \[ s = \hat D\,(L + r) + z \sqrt{(L + r)\,\sigma_D^2 + \hat D^2\,\sigma_L^2} \]

    where \(\hat D\) is the forecast per day, \(L\) the delivery time, \(r\) the review period, \(\sigma_D^2\) and \(\sigma_L^2\) the variances of daily demand and delivery time, and \(z\) the safety factor set by the service target (for example 95% → z ≈ 1.64). This is the usual safety-stock formula 3. 3. Order size Q = S − s. Chosen so that ordering costs and holding costs are balanced, in the style of the economic order quantity (EOQ) 4, then allowed to vary. 4. Never too small for the children. A warehouse's s is at least the biggest order one of its children places, so a single child order never empties it by surprise.

Every site starts the simulation with S units on the shelf.

docs.title: 6. Factory capacity
docs.text:
A factory makes one batch at a time. The batch size is set so that, on a normal day, the factory is busy 60% to 97% of the time. For comparison, Indian manufacturing as a whole ran at 74.6% of capacity in early 2026 6.

Capacity is sized for normal demand. The busy season and demand growth can push a factory above its limit. How far is recorded in peak_load (above 1 means it cannot keep up at the peak).

docs.title: 7. Limited suppliers
docs.text:
In half of the setups, some suppliers are limited. They produce raw material at a fixed rate (3% to 67% above their normal flow) into a store of limited size. If factories need more than that for long enough, the supplier runs out.

The store holds 7 to 30 days of flow, and at least enough to fill the largest single order a factory can ever send it. That second rule matters: in SupplyNetPy an order is shipped whole, so an order bigger than the whole store could never be filled and the factory would stop for good.

docs.title: 8. Breakdowns
docs.text:
In 60% of setups, each supplier, factory and warehouse (without its own customers) may break down, with a chance of 20% to 70% per site. A site that can break down does so every 180 to 1,500 days on average, and each breakdown lasts 2 to 30 days on average. The time between breakdowns is random (exponential). Breakdown lengths have a long tail, so a rare breakdown can last several months. For comparison, the 2021 fire at the Renesas Naka chip plant took about 97 days to recover from 7.

During a breakdown a site takes no new orders. Shipments already on the road still arrive.

docs.title: The four industries
docs.text:
The rules above are the same for every industry. Only the ranges change:

Groceries (FMCG) Electronics Medicines (pharma) Industrial spare parts Typical demand per customer stream 40 units/day 8 units/day 15 units/day 2 units/day Customer orders per day 2–6 0.5–2 1–3 0.1–0.8 (few, large orders) Delivery time, supplier → factory 2–10 days 14–45 days 30–90 days 7–30 days Delivery time, factory → warehouse 1–5 days 5–30 days 3–10 days 3–14 days Delivery time, warehouse → shop 1–3 days 2–7 days 1–4 days 2–7 days Raw material price per unit 0.2–2 10–120 2–40 20–400 Shop price ÷ factory cost 1.5–2.4 1.3–2.0 1.8–4.5 1.6–3.5 Holding cost per year (share of value) 10%–30% 10%–40% 10%–30% 10%–35% Average service target 50%–99% 50%–98% 70%–99.5% 50%–98% Freight (share of goods value) 1%–3% 0.5%–2% 0.3%–1% 1%–3% Unit consumer pack device strip / pack part

Money has no currency. Each setup uses its own price units, set by its raw-material price.

Where these ranges come from

The ranges are reasoned design choices, chosen to be plausible for each industry and wide enough to give variety. They are not fitted to data. The few that were checked against public figures are listed in Assumptions and limits.

docs.title: How a simulation runs
docs.text: A setup (a network with all its numbers) is handed to SupplyNetPy and played out for 5 years (1,825 days). One such play-out is a run. This page explains how long a run is, how many runs each setup gets, and what is measured.

docs.title: The whole pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Pick sizes"] --> B["Make networks<br/>(up to 50 per size)"]
    B --> C["For each network × each of 4 industries:<br/>one base setup"]
    C --> D{"Chosen for extra<br/>copies?"}
    D -- "25% of base setups" --> E["+ 2 what-if copies"]
    D -- "otherwise" --> F["base setup only"]
    E --> G{"Chosen for repeats?"}
    F --> G
    G -- "10%" --> H["5 runs each"]
    G -- "90%" --> I["1 run each"]
    H --> J["Simulate 1,825 days"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["Measure years 2–5"]
    K --> L["Write tables"]

Everything random comes from one starting number (the seed). The same seed always gives the same dataset, on any computer and with any number of parallel workers.

docs.title: One run, day by day
docs.text:
1. Build the SupplyNetPy network from the setup.
  2. Give every node, link and customer stream its own random stream. This keeps them independent, and it is what makes the what-if copies fair (see below).
  3. For each day 1 … 1,825: run the simulation to the end of the day, then record the network's totals for that day: demand, sales, stock, money in and money out.
  4. At the end of the warm-up and at the end of the run, record every node's counters.
  5. Work out the results (below).

docs.title: Why 5 years, and why throw away the first
docs.text:
Every site starts with a full shelf (S units), and that stock is free. The first year is therefore unrealistically good: in a pilot study, year 1 showed a profit margin 8.4 percentage points too high. From year 2 on, results settled within ±0.6 points of later years. So:

  • Year 1 is warm-up. It is simulated, but left out of every result.
  • Years 2 to 5 are measured. That is 4 whole years, so every season is counted the same number of times and seasonal demand does not bias the averages.

Four measured years were enough to make the typical run's profit estimate accurate to within about 1% of its revenue. A fifth year would have improved that by only 0.1 points for 25% more computing.

Each run also gets an automatic warm-up check, MSER-5 1. It finds the point after which the weekly profit series looks settled. The column warmup_ok says whether that point falls inside the first year.

docs.title: Repeats: how much is luck?
docs.text: 10% of base setups are run 5 times with the same numbers but different random luck (different customer arrivals, delivery times and breakdowns). This shows how much a result changes by chance alone. In the demo build, the fill rate of the best and worst of 5 repeats differed by about 2 percentage points.

docs.title: What-if copies: cause and effect
docs.text:
25% of base setups get 2 what-if copies. A copy is the same setup with exactly one change:

Change What is done Breakdown One supplier, factory or warehouse is shut for 14–90 days, starting at a random day in the measured years Smaller factory One factory's batch size is cut to 30%–90% Different safety stock One site's safety factor z is raised or lowered by 0.5–1.5

The copy uses the same random luck as its base: the very same customers arrive at the very same times. So the difference between a copy and its base is caused by the change alone. The columns variant, variant_node, variant_start and variant_value describe the change, and base_config_id points to the base.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
All results cover the measured window only (years 2–5).

For the whole network (runs table, columns starting with main_):

Result Meaning main_fill Fill rate: share of customer demand served straight from the shelf main_profit_day Profit per day: sales to customers minus all costs (raw material, making, holding, freight). Sales between sites of the same network cancel out main_margin Profit ÷ sales main_ext_revenue_day Sales to customers per day main_holding_day, main_transport_day, main_raw_day, main_mfg_day The cost parts main_avg_inventory Average units in stock at factories, warehouses and shops main_stockout_share Share of days a customer-facing site ended with an empty shelf main_outage_days Total days of breakdown, over all nodes

For every node (node_results table): its own fill rate, demand, shortage, units shipped, average stock, money in and out, breakdown days and, for factories and warehouses, the real delivery time it saw.

Day by day (series table): the network's daily customer demand, sales, revenue, cost, profit, stock and unshipped orders, for all 1,825 days, warm-up included.

docs.title: Results at a glance
docs.text:
Industry Group Runs Typical fill rate Fill rate below 0.7 Losing money Typical margin Groceries (FMCG) stress 5,706 0.84 19.0% 4.2% 0.29 Groceries (FMCG) control 1,573 0.96 3.2% 0.0% 0.44 Electronics stress 5,799 0.80 28.0% 12.8% 0.19 Electronics control 1,271 0.96 3.1% 0.2% 0.33 Medicines (pharma) stress 5,886 0.88 10.3% 1.2% 0.49 Medicines (pharma) control 1,574 0.98 5.7% 0.0% 0.65 Industrial spare parts stress 5,860 0.80 22.0% 7.3% 0.36 Industrial spare parts control 1,506 0.94 2.2% 0.2% 0.53

Typical means the median. Fill rate below 0.7 means less than 70% of customer demand was served.

Stress setups fail much more often than control setups, as intended. Electronics loses money most often, because its margins are the thinnest.

docs.text:
A 5-year run takes about 0.07 seconds of computer time per node: about 3.5 s for a 50-node network and 10 s for a 150-node one.

Spratt, "A comparison of five steady-state truncation heuristics for simulation", Proceedings of the 2000 Winter Simulation Conference. ↩

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
SupplyNetPy is an open-source Python library for building and simulating supply chains 1. It is developed at IIT Goa by Tushar Lone, Lekshmi P and Prof. Neha Karanjkar, and is free to use from PyPI (pip install supplynetpy).

It is a discrete-event simulator: instead of moving the clock forward in fixed steps and checking everything, it jumps from one event to the next (an order arrives, a truck delivers, a machine finishes a batch). This is exact and fast. It is built on SimPy, a well-known Python library for this kind of simulation 2.

docs.title: Why it is useful here
docs.text:
• Any network shape. A supply chain is described as a list of nodes and links, so a program can build thousands of different networks automatically. This was one of the library's design goals 1.
  • Ready-made parts. Suppliers, factories, warehouses, customers, delivery links, stock rules and breakdowns already exist and are tested. We do not write a simulator from scratch.
  • Checked against known answers. Its authors validated it against textbook formulas, a commercial simulation tool and a published case study 1.
  • Detailed statistics. Every node keeps counters (units ordered, shipped, lost, money spent and earned), which we read out to build the results.

Before using it at scale, we tested it on many networks and reported 11 issues in multi-level networks upstream (issue #1 and pull request #2 on the SupplyNetPy GitHub). They were fixed in versions 0.2.0 and 0.2.1. This dataset uses version 0.2.2, pinned, with no changes to the library 3.

docs.title: How it is used
docs.text:
Each simulated supply chain is handed to SupplyNetPy as three lists: nodes, links and demands. The parts used are:

SupplyNetPy part Used for What we set infinite_supplier A supplier that never runs out raw-material price supplier (finite) A supplier that produces raw material at a fixed rate into a limited store rate, store size manufacturer A factory that turns raw materials into the product, one batch at a time recipe, batch size, batch time, stock rule, costs warehouse A distribution centre (DC) or shop that holds stock and reorders stock rule, buy and sell price, holding cost Link A delivery route between two nodes delivery-time distribution, cost per order Demand A stream of customer orders at a shop when orders arrive, how big they are SSReplenishment The stock rule at every factory, DC and shop: the (s, S) policy reorder level s, order-up-to level S, review period node disruption Random or planned breakdowns when they start, how long they last

One part is our own: WeightedSelect, a small supplier-choice rule. When a site has two suppliers, it sends each order to one of them at random, using fixed weights (for example 70% / 30%). It is written as a SupplyNetPy SupplierSelectionPolicy, the library's intended way to extend this.

A tiny example of the same building blocks (adapted from the SupplyNetPy quick start 4):

import SupplyNetPy.Components as scm

supplier = {"ID": "S1", "name": "Supplier", "node_type": "infinite_supplier"}
shop = {"ID": "R1", "name": "Shop", "node_type": "warehouse",
        "capacity": float("inf"), "initial_level": 50, "inventory_holding_cost": 0.2,
        "replenishment_policy": scm.SSReplenishment, "policy_param": {"s": 40, "S": 120},
        "product_buy_price": 100, "product_sell_price": 105}
link = {"ID": "L1", "source": "S1", "sink": "R1", "cost": 5, "lead_time": lambda: 2}
customers = {"ID": "d1", "name": "Customers", "demand_node": "R1",
             "order_arrival_model": lambda: 1, "order_quantity_model": lambda: 10}

net = scm.create_sc_net(nodes=[supplier, shop], links=[link], demands=[customers])
net["env"].run(until=365)            # one simulated year
print(net["nodes"]["R1"].stats.demand_fulfilled)

The dataset does the same thing, at a larger scale and with every number filled in by rules:

flowchart LR
    G["network + numbers<br/>(generator/chain.py: configure)"] --> N["nodes, links, demands<br/>(chain.netlist)"]
    N --> C["scm.create_sc_net"]
    C --> R["run one day at a time<br/>env.run(until=t)"]
    R --> S["read every node's<br/>statistics each day"]
    S --> R
    S --> O["daily history +<br/>results tables"]

Running one day at a time lets us record the network's daily history (sales, stock, profit) without changing anything inside SupplyNetPy.

Settings that keep the simulation safe

A few library features are used in a fixed way, to avoid known edge cases: customers never wait (unserved demand is lost), recipes use whole numbers, and site storage space is unlimited (factories are limited by how fast they can produce instead). See Assumptions and limits.

  2. SimPy, discrete-event simulation for Python. https://simpy.readthedocs.io/ ↩

  3. SupplyNetPy source code and issue tracker. https://github.com/SupplyChainSimulation/SupplyNetPy ↩

  4. SupplyNetPy documentation. https://supplychainsimulation.github.io/SupplyNetPy/ ↩
